entries.title: 2 killed, 1 hurt in Amtrak train crash in Western Springs
entries.summary: <p>An Amtrak train collided with a vehicle Wednesday morning at a railway crossing in west suburban Western Springs, leaving two people dead and at least one injured. </p><p>At 8 a.m., Amtrak train No. 381, westbound from Chicago to Quincy, hit a vehicle on the tracks at Wolf Road in Western Springs, according to Amtrak and a statement from the village of Western Springs, about 20 miles west of Chicago. No other details were provided, such as whether the crossing arms were lowered at the time of the collision.</p><p>Two people in the vehicle were killed, and another person was transported to Loyola University Medical Center in Maywood, according to the statement. </p><p>The Cook County medical examiner's office had not released their names or other details as of noon Wednesday.</p><p>None of the 35 passengers and crew were hurt, Amtrak said.</p><p>Train customers were moved to a bus to continue west, with that bus making all of the regular train stops between La Grange and Quincy, according to Amtrak. </p><p>Several law enforcement and emergency response teams were on site as the investigation continues. </p><p>Crossings at Grand Avenue and Wolf Road are closed, but Lawn Avenue remains open. All traffic and pedestrians should avoid the area until further notice. </p><p>Those tracks are also used by Metra's BNSF line, which announced significant cancellations, warning passengers that crowding on remaining trains could be severe and to plan on alternate transportation if possible, according to the Metra website. A Metra spokesperson said that while the tracks were fine and some trains had passed through Wednesday night, crew rest hour requirements could carry over delays into early Thursday, though service would likely be close to normal.</p><p>As a result, inbound and outbound BNSF trains would travel only between Union Station and La Grange Road, and between Aurora and Hinsdale. No train service will be provided between Stone Avenue and Highlands, according to a service alert on the Metra website.</p><p>As of Wednesday night, Western Springs had not provided any updates on the accident.</p>

entries.title: Bulls rookie Caleb Wilson answers the bell ... at least until 2nd half
entries.summary: <p>The growing pains continue for Caleb Wilson.</p><p>At least on Wednesday, literally.</p><p>The Bulls’ prized rookie was questionable to answer the bell against the Spurs, dealing with a sore hip in the wake of the loss to Philadelphia on Sunday. It was enough of a concern that he needed to get through warmups, test it out, and then give the medical staff the nod that he was good to go.</p><p>He did play well in his 15 minutes of work, scoring 15 points on 5-of-7 shooting, but injured his right hand and did not return to the game in the second half.</p><p>A reminder to the Bulls that leading the team with 32.4 minutes per game was necessary for the development piece that the No. 4 overall draft pick needs, but maybe a stat they want to keep a little closer eye on for the next few games.</p><p>“We’ve got to be smart with him of course,” coach Tiago Splitter said of Wilson. “He’s playing a lot of minutes. Those minutes are important to his development, but we’ve also got to be smart with his body being young. I think there’s a false thought that when you’re young you can do whatever but that’s not true. You’ve got to get stronger, you’ve got to get your body prepared to face a season like the NBA, so we’ve got to be careful there and we’ve got to monitor it for sure.”</p><p>Wilson played 32 minutes against the 76ers and was coming off a game in New York in which he had a soft benching in New York because of body language and a lack of resiliency in Splitter’s estimation. He only put in a season-low 22 minutes in that loss until leaving the Spurs game early.</p><p>But even with those moments for the 20-year-old where he might take one step back, there’s been way more moments of taking steps forward through the first 10 games.</p><p>“Honestly every game is a little bit different,” Splitter said of the Wilson’s growth so far. “He did some great things, and other games he wasn’t as good, but again, it’s not like a (upward) line. It’s up and down, up and down, and you grow, right. I think he’s working hard, he’s doing everything we ask. There are a lot of things on his plate right now, learning different things, and he’s grown, he’s getting better.”</p><p><b>The Claxton Effect</b></p><p></p><p>The sample size is small – just two games to be exact – but veteran big man Nic Claxton’s presence was being felt on both ends of the floor.</p><p>Claxton, who was acquired in an offseason four-team trade, was sidelined since the start of training camp with a strained hamstring. He made his Bulls debut in the Sunday loss to the 76ers, coming off the bench because of minutes restrictions, and was again in that role against San Antonio.</p><p>One player that’s really appreciated having Claxton behind him protecting the rim? Second-year forward Noa Essengue.</p><p>“That’s one of the best feelings, honestly,” Essengue said. “Because I know I can make a mistake because I have someone behind me to protect me, so it’s just amazing.</p><p>“I just know I can do a little more. I can put a little more pressure on the ball, try more deflections.”</p><p></p><p><b>A vet down</b></p><p></p><p>Norman Powell missed his second consecutive game, still dealing with back spasms.</p><p>The good news for the Bulls and their veteran shooting guard? It doesn’t sound like he’ll be in street clothes much longer.</p><p>“He’s around 70%, not ready to go, but expecting him to be ready next game,” Splitter said.</p><p>With Powell sidelined, the Bulls again turned to veteran wing Isaac Okoro. Okoro also started Sunday’s game against the 76ers, finishing with 12 points and a plus-1 in plus/minus.</p>

entries.title: Taking care of business: Chicago's first self-cleaning public restroom opens in Polish Triangle
entries.summary: <p>Christian Malatesta wanted to go first.</p><p>When he heard the 1st Ward, where he lives, was getting Chicago's first self-cleaning public restroom, Malatesta emailed Ald. Daniel La Spata to ask for the first spot in line.</p><p>Malatesta, 35, had used a similar facility in Paris, and was excited to see the technology come to Chicago.</p><p>“I don't think you should have to buy a $5 cup of coffee to use the restroom,” he said.</p><p>His big moment arrived Wednesday, when La Spata and JCDecaux, the company providing and operating the facility, officially opened it to the public.</p><p>Located near the CTA's Division Street Blue Line station, the facility is designed for one user at a time. Visitors press a button to open the sliding door. Inside, there's a bright blue wall and a map of Chicago and plenty of space to move about comfortably. When they've left, an integrated system washes and disinfects the toilet and floor after each use.</p><p>Malatesta got his wish, and headed in. The experience, he said, was straightforward.</p><p>“Everything was labeled very clearly, and everything was where I expected it to be,” Malatesta said. “You just press the button, the door opens for you, it flushes for you.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-280000" name="image-280000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4ba04b4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F15%2Fe4%2Faa37d56d4975b51b827a77d3ad52%2Fwesttowntoilet-261112-18.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0618aea/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F15%2Fe4%2Faa37d56d4975b51b827a77d3ad52%2Fwesttowntoilet-261112-18.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4582bd6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F15%2Fe4%2Faa37d56d4975b51b827a77d3ad52%2Fwesttowntoilet-261112-18.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ald. entries.title: What to know about CPS and AI as Chicago students risk losing access to Google search
entries.summary: <p>It's AI’s world and we’re just living in it.</p><p>At least that’s what the last couple of years have felt like as artificial intelligence creeps into gadgets, software, media and other aspects of our lives. Some school districts, such as New York and Los Angeles, have responded by banning AI for some students.</p><p>In Chicago Public Schools, students aren’t allowed access to popular AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, Google’s Gemini and other generative AI programs because of privacy and safety concerns.</p><p>But that doesn’t mean teachers and students aren’t using AI. The school district has released guidance for educators and students for the last two years on how they can adopt the technology in teaching and learning. The guidance says it prioritizes “human oversight” while promoting and encouraging “experimentation” of district-approved AI tools to enhance what students get out of the classroom.</p><p>The framework gives students examples of how to use the technology, such as creating study guides and generating images about a chapter of a book they are reading. It suggests ways teachers can use AI to get rid of “busy work” and spend more time with students.</p><p>At the same time, a growing chorus of parents want to put the brakes on the district’s embrace of AI and minimize screen time for students, citing concerns that it could be affecting their learning.</p><p>As the district continues to grapple with the fast-evolving technology it also has to deal with a new issue. Last week <a class="Link" href="https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/education/ai-learning-era-updates-2026/" target="_blank" ><u>Google announced</u></a> that next year school districts that choose to forego its AI products will lose access to Google search.</p><p>That puts CPS in a major bind and helped fuel a protest in front of Google’s West Loop office on Wednesday. Students use Google search for homework, research and other assignments. The district also relies on other Google products, such as Google Classroom, Google Drive and Google Docs. Finding alternatives would be a big undertaking.</p><p>Here are a few things to know about the district’s approach to AI.</p><p><b>Why are Chicago Public Schools students at risk of losing Google search?</b></p><p>Earlier this month Google <a class="Link" href="https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/education/ai-learning-era-updates-2026/" target="_blank" ><u>announced updates to its suite of programs</u></a> that use AI, including Google Classroom and Gemini Notebook, an AI research tool. Access will be automatically turned off for K-12 students until administrators turn them on.</p><p>But Chris Phillips, vice president of education at Google, in <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/us/google-search-schools-restrict-ai.html?unlocked_article_code=1.NlE.VMKr.Cr-g-C6phyfH&smid=url-share" target="_blank" ><u>an interview with the New York Times</u></a>, said that schools that ban AI entirely “will not have access to search” because “search and AI are deeply engrained.”</p><p>The district has “not yet determined its response to Google's announced search engine restriction,” a CPS spokesperson said in a statement.</p><p>CPS is “actively exploring all options to independently suppress” the AI mode amid those constraints, the statement said. “The District would like to continue to provide students with access to the Google search engine without the AI component. If such an arrangement can’t be reached, the District will look to other search solutions.”</p><p>In a statement, a Google spokesperson said the company is updating its AI search features for classrooms so it gives step-by-step instructions on how to solve problems instead of just “quick answers.” The statement didn’t address the protest or answer questions about cutting off search.</p><p>New York and LA, which enacted strict restrictions on AI use in schools, are in the same boat as Chicago. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said “no corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children.”</p><p>Google is by far the dominant provider of education technology for U.S. schools. class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p><b>What do we mean when we talk about AI?</b></p><p>In general, whenever someone discusses AI in schools they are referring to Generative AI, a subset of artificial intelligence that generates new content such as text, audio, code, images or video. These outputs are based on data that is typically derived from the internet.</p><p>Users input specific requests via text prompts to generate the content. This usually takes the form of a chatbot. Popular programs include Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini.</p><p><b>What is CPS’ AI policy?</b></p><p>The district doesn’t have a binding policy on the use of the technology within CPS. Instead, the district <a class="Link" href="https://www.cps.edu/globalassets/cps-pages/initiatives/ai-guidebook/cps-ai-guidebook.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>has released guidelines</u></a> for educator use in their classrooms. CPS has said it chose to first develop guidance rather than policy because that gave it the flexibility to adapt to the fast-evolving nature of the technology.</p><p>The district released its first version in 2024, around the time AI chatbots were becoming more widely used. It was among the first districts in the state to release guidance. The guidelines have been updated several times but the core principles have remained the same.</p><p>They aim to ensure that “AI augments, rather than replaces, the essential role of educators.” The district has an online database of approved AI tools. Teachers that use the tools are also responsible for monitoring how students are using them.</p><p>That means that staff have to review any results from an AI tool for accuracy or biases. The guidelines also advise staff to only enter confidential information — such as student records and any identifying information — into AI tools that have privacy agreements with the district.</p><p>This year the district released a <a class="Link" href="https://www.cps.edu/globalassets/cps-pages/initiatives/ai-guidebook/instructional-genai-playbook.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>“GenAI Playbook”</u></a> that provides examples of how teachers can use the technology. It recommends teachers think about “busy work” that AI can help with so they have more time with students. It suggests teachers use AI to help draft progress reports, incident logs or put together meeting minutes.</p><p>The playbook also includes ways teachers can integrate approved AI tools in their lessons. For example, teachers can use AI to create an interactive podcast version of a textbook chapter and have students chime in.</p><p><b>How are students using AI in the classroom? </b></p><p>That can depend on the school, the teachers, parents and the tools themselves. Currently students do not have direct access to AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude and Google’s Gemini. The district blocks access to those tools on student accounts.</p><p>“With the exception of Google Search's default AI Mode, which the District is actively working to suppress, CPS does not provide students with access to generative AI applications in order to safeguard student privacy and safety,” a district spokesman said in a statement.</p><p>Parents can also opt their children out of having access to AI tools. Many tools also restrict access for younger students. ChatGPT and Perplexity don’t allow anyone under 13, for example.</p><p>According to the CPS guidelines, students first must get permission from their teacher before using AI tools for academic work and identify any AI-generated content in their assignments. The district reserves the right to take away access to these tools from students who use them irresponsibly.</p><p>The recent AI playbook suggests AI can help with brainstorming, generating timelines and tasks for group projects as well as overcoming writer’s block.</p><p>Students may also use AI to create videos, music and digital media with AI to compliment their learning. One example is for students to use a district-approved tool to create an image based on a chapter of a book they are reading.</p><p>The implementation of this guidance can vary depending on how comfortable teachers are with the technology. Some teachers may welcome the tools, while others may be more reluctant.</p><p>But the guidance doesn’t prevent students from interacting with AI at home. The district’s guidebook acknowledges that, and asks teachers to consider showing students how to responsibly interact with the technology.</p><p><b>Why are some parents asking for a moratorium on AI at CPS?</b></p><p>Google’s announcement also prompted swift backlash from groups that want CPS to enact a 3-year moratorium on AI use in schools and are seeking to limit screen time in classrooms.</p><p>Illinois Families for Public Schools and the local chapter of Schools Beyond Screens held a protest outside Google’s West Loop office on Wednesday. They are also calling on CPS to develop a more clear and consistent policy on AI and for the district to limit screen time in all grades.</p><p>Kimberly Tobin, parent of two young children at Burroughs Elementary, said Google’s announcement felt “like an ultimatum” for school districts.</p><p>“It's more influence than I would like tech companies to have over the types of products that are put in front of our kids,” she said.</p><p>Tobin said research indicates that increased screen time and unrestricted use of AI can affect student’s grades and keep them from developing skills.</p><p>“There's a pretty significant risk of fragmented attention when kids are doing most of their work on a screen,” Tobin said.</p><p>She and Schools Beyond Screens want CPS to look at how technology use impacts learning and develop a clear policy so that AI use doesn’t vary from school to school.</p><p>She noted that while the district restricts use of ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude from students, some of the approved education programs, such as reading assistant Amira, use AI.</p><p>“It's not like we don't want them to have access to any kind of technology, but we want it to be for a purpose,” Tobin said.</p>

entries.title: Bears sending care package after viral social media interaction
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> are sending a care package to an Australian X user after Bears fans reached out in their time of need.</p><p>On Sunday, a social media user by the name of @treatmachanwell wrote a dark post on X: “If I kill myself then I'm just no longer a burden.” Later that night, Bears fans went to the app to search for medical updates on wide receiver Luther Burden, who was concussed on a fumble the fourth quarter. By searching the word “Burden,” they were fed the post. </p><p>Almost 500 people responded encouraging the user to stay upbeat. Many sent photos of Luther Burden or Bears fans inside Soldier Field — which was initially confusing to the social media user.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">HOW DID I GET THIS FAR <a href="https://t.co/naToKajBox">https://t.co/naToKajBox</a> <a href="https://t.co/2dhhekcySE">pic.twitter.com/2dhhekcySE</a></p>— ⋆˚࿔ 𝕐𝕦𝕣𝕚 ♪˚⋆ (@treatmachanwell) <a href="https://x.com/treatmachanwell/status/2120614751919300750?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 11, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>“Ive got no idea who the Chicago Bears are — I'm Australian,” wrote Yuri, whose original post has more than 7 million views.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Extending a special welcome to all the newest members of Bears FC 🫶</p>— Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) <a href="https://x.com/ChicagoBears/status/2120591052361069018?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 11, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Wednesday, the user posted a screen shot of the Bears offering to mail a care package. entries.title: Second man charged in fatal Belmont Cragin stabbing
entries.summary: <p>A second man has been charged in a fatal 2025 stabbing in Belmont Cragin, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Jose Ramos, 25, was charged with first-degree murder and mob action, police said. He was arrested Tuesday.</p><p>Yahir Viveros-Alarcon, 27, died of multiple stab wounds on June 7, 2025, according to the Cook County medical examiner’s office.</p><p>An already injured Viveros-Alarcon walked into a convenience store in the 5600 block of West Fullerton Avenue at 8:45 p.m., where a witness found him, police said. He was taken to Loyola University Medical Center in Maywood, where he was pronounced dead.</p><p>In November 2025, Sergio Vargas, 29, was arrested and charged with murder and mob action in connection with the fatal stabbing.</p><p>Ramos is due in court Thursday.</p>

entries.title: Who said monsters aren't real? Bulls find out hard way with Wemby
entries.summary: <p>Tiago Splitter knows the 7-foot-4 monster all too well.</p><p>After all, the last time the coach saw Victor Wembanyama up close and personal, he was ending the storybook postseason run for Portland last April, throwing a 35-point Game 1 on Splitter’s Trail Blazers and finishing the gentleman’s sweep with four blocks per game.</p><p>So now even with a new team, there were rules Splitter was stressing to his Bulls players the last few days in dealing with the MVP candidate:</p><p>“We’ve got to shoot the ball well,” Splitter insisted. “You’ve got to have a team that is going to shoot the ball well, and sometimes it’s hard to have everything, but to beat the Spurs you’ve got to shoot the ball well from three.”</p><p>A box that was checked in the first half, as the Bulls went 10-of-15 from long range.</p><p>“You’ve got to force (Wembanyama) to get out of the paint,” Splitter continued. “That’s going to create easier shots at the rim. If you just try to get at him the whole game that’s in their favor.”</p><p>Another check through the first two quarters, as the Bulls shot 66% from the field to build a 14-point lead going into the locker room.</p><p>But there’s a reason why the French import continues to change the entire geometry of the game, as the visiting Spurs erased that deficit just six minutes into the second half – and of course Wembanyama was a big reason why – handing the Bulls (1-9) the 124-119 defeat and an eighth-straight loss.</p><p>“We talked about the third quarter before we even went out there,” Splitter said afterward. “We just didn’t have it. We were careless with the ball.”</p><p>The coach didn’t even have to point any fingers because Matas Buzelis took care of that, pointing it at himself and the four of six turnovers he committed in that third quarter alone.</p><p>“Weak with the ball,” Buzelis said. “Mainly me. That’s unacceptable, man. That was our game to win. I feel like I lost that game for us. They turned up the physicality and we didn’t punch back, I didn’t punch back.”</p><p>Wembanyama’s presence didn’t help as he finished with a game-high 32 points and added five blocks.</p><p>No wonder Splitter had nothing but praise for the rising star.</p><p>“I think he’s honestly one of those players that is going to change the game,” Splitter said. “There’s no comp. You can’t comp him to anybody. That could be good or bad, but I think he’s changing the league. He was close to winning a championship last year and I think he’s going to be one of the greatest to ever play this game.”</p><p>The hope was it wasn’t going to be the case on Wednesday. San Antonio was finishing a four-game road trip in Chicago and looked like it had caught up with them, especially in the opening stanza in which the Bulls bench helped build the lead to as much as 13.</p><p>As been the case far too often this season, however, third quarters seem to doom this young Bulls team. The Spurs game was just the latest example of that.</p><p>Maybe it was the visiting team getting its legs back under them or former Bulls coach Billy Donovan – now an assistant with San Antonio – reiterating the weaknesses of his former core players, but it turned ugly quickly.</p><p>Having a paint eraser like Wembanyama didn’t hurt.</p><p>“I mean that’s amazing, not only for French (basketball fans) but for Europe,” Bulls second-year forward Noa Essengue said of his fellow countryman in Wembanyama and his takeover of the league. “That just shows how much talent we have over there. That’s just a great example of that. Not that many people are watching Euro basketball and just the way he has shown up on how much he can impact the league, not only offensively but defensively is just amazing.”</p>

entries.title: Richard Posner, longtime federal judge and 'prolific' University of Chicago legal scholar, dies at 87
entries.summary: <p>Richard Posner, a former federal appellate judge and University of Chicago law scholar who became one of the most cited legal scholars of the 20th century, died Tuesday.</p><p>His death was confirmed by the University of Chicago. He was 87.</p><p>Posner made it known he detested jargon-filled legal writing and leaned into practical solutions for complex legal questions in the nearly 3,300 legal opinions he penned during his 36-year stint on the bench. In his lengthy career, and even into retirement, Posner authored more than 60 books and dozens more legal journal articles.</p><p>University of Chicago Law School Dean Adam Chilton said: “There has never been a legal scholar quite as prolific, influential, and endlessly curious as Dick Posner.”</p><p>“He was a giant whose influence on our legal system, the field of law and economics, and on our law school cannot be overstated,” Chilton said in a <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.uchicago.edu/news/senior-lecturer-richard-posner-law-and-economics-pioneer-and-former-federal-appellate-judge" target="_blank" ><u>statement</u></a>. “As a law and economics scholar and torts professor, I doubt there has been a week that’s gone by since I started teaching at the Law School where I haven’t talked about one of Dick’s ideas or opinions. We will mourn his loss deeply, and on behalf of the entire Law School community, I extend our deepest condolences to his family.”</p><p>Posner’s law journey began as a clerk for Supreme Court Justice William J. Brennan. From 1965 to 1967. He served as assistant to future Supreme Court Justice Thurgood Marshall.</p><p>Posner joined the University of Chicago’s law school in 1969, and just four years later, wrote “Economic Analysis of Law,” largely held as an extremely influential book in the field.</p><p>By 1978, he was made the Lee and Brena Freeman Professor of Law, a role he held until he was appointed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit by President Ronald Reagan in 1981. Posner served as the chief judge from 1993 to 2000.</p><p>Among his thousands of legal opinions were rulings overturning same-sex marriage bans in Indiana and Wisconsin in 2014, along with a 2013 decision to block a Wisconsin abortion ban.</p><p>Posner also wrote the majority opinion in a ruling that struck down an Illinois ban on concealed carrying on public transit, a decision state lawmakers later worked around. He also made his disdain for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/5/14/18407667/we-got-the-right-guys-retired-atf-agent-says-of-controversial-drug-stings" target="_blank" ><u>ATF stash house raids</u></a> known in a 2012 <a class="Link" href="https://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/USCOURTS-ca7-11-02439/pdf/USCOURTS-ca7-11-02439-0.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>dissent</u></a>.</p><p>He later <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2017/9/2/18375672/judge-posner-one-of-world-s-leading-public-intellectuals-retires" target="_blank" ><u>retired</u></a> from the bench in 2017, saying he looked forward “to continuing to teach and publish, with a particular focus on social justice reform.”</p><p>“I am proud to have promoted a pragmatic approach to judging during my time on the Court, and to have had the opportunity to apply my view that judicial opinions should be easy to understand and that judges should focus on the right and wrong in every case,” Posner said in a statement at the time of his retirement.</p><p>He is survived by his wife Charlene, two sons and four grandchildren. The details of services are pending.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Inviting sibling’s ex-husband to graduation party tore family apart
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My sister, "Randee," and I are experiencing a falling-out with our older brother, "Darren," which has left us hurt and confused. We come from a large, tightly knit family, and there's always some sort of celebration happening. We siblings are in our 40s and 50s, so there are also lots of nieces and nephews.</p><p>Darren and his wife planned a small graduation party for their son and invited Randee's ex-husband, who was a complete monster during their recent divorce. Randee and I didn't want to be around him at all. Darren and his wife were aware of this but invited him anyway. Although Darren has a long-term friendship with Randee's ex, we were still upset that he chose him over us.</p><p>When I approached Darren about the situation and asked him nicely to have us come earlier and the ex come later, he reacted with anger and told us not to come at all! He later told us never to contact him again and that we are cut off from his children as well.</p><p>It has been nine months, and he hasn't shown up to any family functions. When I saw my nephew at the park, he ignored me as if I didn't exist. That hurt a lot, considering how close we always were. Darren refuses to apologize or make amends, and he stews in anger over it. His wife and children have joined his anger-fest as well. My parents spent their whole lives keeping us all together and making the holidays and celebrations special. They are heartbroken as well. How do we proceed? — <i>BROKEN IN NEW YORK</i></p><p><b>DEAR BROKEN:</b> From what you have written, I suspect there may be more turmoil in your family than you mentioned in your letter. Start trying to mend fences by apologizing to Darren for dictating who he could or could not entertain at his son's graduation celebration. Darren did not choose his friend over you and Randee. He chose all three of you, and you chose to create drama where it didn't need to exist.</p><p>As the host, he, not you, was rightly in charge of his guest list. To enjoy the same graduation party as Randee's ex, all you had to do was avoid talking to him without making an announcement or making it obvious. This is what polite people do if they fear they will encounter an uncomfortable situation.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> What is the rule of etiquette for waving to neighbors? I wave to some who never return the wave. Is it OK to stop waving to them? Should I wait until somebody waves to wave back? I feel like a fool waving to the same people who never wave back. — <i>NEED WAVE GUIDANCE</i></p><p><b>DEAR WAVE:</b> There's no harm in waving to someone who doesn't reciprocate, but if it makes you uncomfortable, there's also no reason to continue. Are you otherwise on good terms with these neighbors? Do you ever pause for a chat or have them over for dinner? If you rarely or never speak to them, they may not feel your relationship warrants a wave.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Trump second-guesses mass deportations but still sticks with Stephen Miller
entries.summary: <p>In a "60 Minutes" <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/read-the-full-transcript-of-ross-douthats-interview-with-president-trump/" target="_blank" >interview</a> that aired Sunday night, President Donald Trump <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/11/09/trumps-immigration-indecision/" target="_blank" >conceded</a> that his mass deportation campaign may have contributed to the <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/11/03/trump-enters-his-george-w-bush-era-as-democrats-sweep-house-and-senate/" target="_blank" >Republican rout</a> in last week's midterm elections because "a lot of people think it's too tough." Yet on the same day he sat for the interview, Trump <a class="Link" href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117571000109141399" target="_blank" >announced</a> that he had picked Stephen Miller, the main architect of that policy, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.</p><p>Those seemingly contradictory signals reflect a conflict between Trump's "tough" instincts on immigration and his intermittent <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/07/08/trump-reiterates-his-promise-to-protect-farm-and-hospitality-workers-from-pretty-vicious-deportation/" target="_blank" >qualms</a> about the economic and human consequences of deporting unauthorized but otherwise law-abiding residents with deep roots in their communities. Trump's <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/07/02/us/politics/trump-undocumented-immigrants-farmers-hotels.html" target="_blank" >ambivalence</a> jibes with the <a class="Link" href="https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2025/06/17/americans-have-mixed-to-negative-views-of-trump-administration-immigration-actions/" target="_blank" >mixed views</a> of voters, who generally applaud efforts to police the border and expel criminals but are <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/07/16/americans-want-order-not-cruelty-at-the-border/" target="_blank" >less comfortable</a> with deporting <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/01/29/stephen-millers-hardline-immigration-tactics-are-backfiring/" target="_blank" >peaceful and productive people</a> who have worked and raised families in the United States for years.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://transcripts.cnn.com/show/acd/date/2025-07-03/segment/01" target="_blank" >Trump</a> and his <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/feb/22/us-immigration-trump-administration" target="_blank" >underlings</a> have said his immigration crackdown focuses on "the worst of the worst." Yet the Cato Institute's David Bier, who looked at detainees arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in fiscal year 2026, <a class="Link" href="https://www.cato.org/blog/5-ice-detainees-have-violent-convictions-73-no-convictions" target="_blank" >found</a> that 73% had <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/12/12/the-feds-worst-of-the-worst-database-is-stuffed-with-nonviolent-offenders-who-exactly-is-ice-arresting/" target="_blank" >no criminal convictions</a>, nearly half also had no pending criminal charges, and just 5% had been convicted of violent offenses.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-460000" name="module-460000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>The Migration Policy Institute <a class="Link" href="https://www.migrationpolicy.org/publication/us-deportations-second-trump" target="_blank" >reported</a> similar findings in October: During the first 18 months of Trump's second term, just one-fifth of deportees had been convicted of crimes. The organization also noted that 61% of deportees had lived in the U.S. for more than two years, while 15% had been here for a decade or more.</p><p>Although hard-liners like Miller want to "get everybody out," Trump noted in the "60 Minutes" interview, "a lot of people" think the government should deport "the rough ones," including "drug dealers," "rapists" and "killers," but "work a deal" for others, including immigrants who "in some cases" have been here for "10 and 15 years." He said a deal along those lines with the Democrats who will soon take control of Congress is "actually doable."</p><p>This is not the first time that Trump has expressed reservations about the <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/06/11/stephen-millers-dream/" target="_blank" >indiscriminate approach</a> to immigration enforcement favored by Miller. In June 2025, Trump <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/06/16/ice-on-ice/" target="_blank" >ordered</a> a short-lived pause on workplace raids, and the following month he <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/07/08/trump-reiterates-his-promise-to-protect-farm-and-hospitality-workers-from-pretty-vicious-deportation/" target="_blank" >said</a> that "we're gonna work with" employers of unauthorized immigrants in the agriculture and hospitality industries.</p><p>"These people … work so hard," Trump said at a July 2025 <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C9nJFdFBhHA" target="_blank" >rally</a> in Des Moines, Iowa. "They bend over all day. We don't have too many people [who] can do that."</p><p>Trump added that "some of the farmers … cry when they see [immigration raids] happen." He alluded to "cases where … people have worked for a farmer on a farm for 14, 15 years" and "then they get thrown out, pretty viciously."</p><p>Trump's conclusion: "We can't do it. We've got to work with the farmers and people that have hotels and leisure properties."</p><p>Trump revisited that theme on "60 Minutes." When "you have a woman" who is doing "a great job" as a waitress or a hotel cleaner, he said, "and all of a sudden, they're being taken out of the country, it's tough. It's a tough thing."</p><p>Last April, the Pew Research Center <a class="Link" href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/05/04/about-half-of-americans-continue-to-say-trump-administration-is-doing-too-much-on-deportations/" target="_blank" >reported</a> that 52% of Americans thought the Trump administration was doing "too much" when "it comes to deporting immigrants who are living in the U.S. illegally." In a CBS News <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/cbs-news-exit-polls-2026-midterms-democrats/" target="_blank" >exit poll</a> last week, 58% of voters said the Trump administration's immigration enforcement had "gone too far."</p><p>They could be right, Trump admitted in the interview: "It might be too tough." While "I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out," he said, "I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs" whose "one violation" was that "they came into the country illegally."</p><p>Will Trump follow through on these impulses? That depends on the outcome of his debate with Miller — and with himself.</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-eb0000" name="module-eb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. </div> </div><p>Started in 2000, “The Mysterious Production of Eggs” was a Herculean effort that developed over an arduous five-year journey and three distinct stops and starts and came during a time of "immense change and personal challenge." In the beginning, Bird went so far as to abandon city life and build a studio in an 1890s barn his family owned in the northern Illinois village of Elizabeth to get perspective. As he tinkered away at the lush jazz-folk-pop album, his audience was farm chickens, raccoons and a random peacock that showed up at one point.</p><p> “It was really, really isolating, more than I expected,” he said of the sojourn. “I was 29 when this whole adventure started. … It was really a retreat from the canopy of trees and apartment buildings of the Chicago landscape and a bit from the Chicago music community at a time when people were saying you should think about going to New York or L.A.” </p><p>Back then, the classically trained violinist lived in Uptown, taking gigs at the Green Mill and Hideout and teaching classes at the Old Town School of Folk Music. He had already done stints with Squirrel Nut Zippers and established his acclaimed baroque pop group Andrew Bird’s Bowl of Fire (also featuring members like Nora O’Connor and Kevin O'Donnell).</p><p>But Bird wasn't feeling totally fulfilled and desired to retool his career. Doing so took a process of “trying to rewire my brain,” he said. “I had something in my head, and I wasn't sure how to get it yet … I kept thinking, I'm totally failing at this.”</p><div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>For Andrew Bird, a classically trained violinist who was in the Chicago Youth Symphony Orchestra, performing with the CSO is “kind of a big deal for me,” he said.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Reuben Cox</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p> A lot of it had to do with the formal way he was taught to play music, Bird said, starting with the Suzuki method when he was 4 years old. “[Teachers] were like, just follow the program, then you can do what you want. And I'm like, but I see so many people around me follow the program to the point where they've forgotten what it is to access that creativity and imagination and they lose it. I was just trying to hang on until I got away from the system and could do what I wanted.”</p><p>Like packing up everything and moving to the same barn where he and his brother used to build caves in the haystacks. Being back in the barn allowed Bird to tap into a similar childlike wonder where he relied on instinct and imagination. “It's the closest I've come to doing a concept album, but not intentionally,” Bird said. “I kept envisioning a [creator of “Where the Wild Things Are”] Maurice Sendak-type kid with the cape and wandering through this adult world that's trying to test and measure this kid and kind of squelch the childhood imagination.” That effect comes across in playful songs like "Opposite Day" and carries into the cartoonish artwork, by local illustrator Jay Ryan, which was expanded in a 20th anniversary box set and a new <a class="Link" href="https://www.andrewbird.net/eggs" target="_blank" ><u>interactive website</u></a> that explores not just the painstaking labor behind the album but also the rewards that came from it.</p><p>Eventually finished in L.A. with the help of producer Tony Berg and engineer David Boucher (and after a soft launch with the 2003 album “Weather Systems”), “The Mysterious Production of Eggs” became a hallmark of early millennium indie folk. Songs like the eclectic “Fake Palindromes” set a precedent for Bird’s 17 whimsical albums and wide-leaping composition work that followed, including pieces for FX comedy "Baskets," "The Muppets” and “The Pitt,” for which he won an Emmy in September.</p><p>The album also had one other big effect — it introduced his trademark whistling, a trick he first learned as a child from his grandmother. </p><p> “I remember going out in the ravines in Lake Bluff and trying to trick the birds into thinking that I was a bird. I would try to imitate their calls,” he said with a laugh. But the trick came in handy professionally around the time he started touring behind “The Mysterious Production of Eggs” as a proverbial one-man band, looping sounds to fill the gaps. </p><p>“As I went from like a five-piece band to solo around the turn of the century,” he said. “I found myself in a situation of having to engage the audience in any way and whatever I had to work with.” He would start the show appropriately with “First Song,” holding the track’s whistling intro as long as he could to get attention. And it worked. “You'd hear the chatter in the crowd just start to die down. Like, is that a smoke alarm? What is that?” he recalled. “The whistle is like glass that just cuts right through everything.”</p><p>Nowadays, Bird has been using flutes to help double that sound effect for “The Mysterious Production of Eggs” concerts. He reworked the songs into full orchestral arrangements with the help of Minneapolis-based composer Nathan Thatcher with the goal of performing the album with symphonies around the country. In Chicago, it marks a particularly special accomplishment — his debut with the CSO this month. “I was in the Chicago Youth Symphony Orchestra, and I studied with Blair Milton, who was in the orchestra and at Northwestern [Bird’s alma mater]. So, this is kind of a big deal for me,” he said.</p><p> Reconfiguring the album into symphonic works admittedly “didn't take that much,” said Bird, who is among recent artists like St. Vincent and Billy Corgan to do so. “The album is already kind of orchestral in some ways. … it makes more sense than any other record.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" on “The Mysterious Production of Eggs.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Andrea Troolin</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>He did enjoy adding new sounds that didn't appear on the original recordings like woodwinds such as the bassoon. “It was not something that was in my toolbox when I was making the album.”</p><p>Ultimately, Bird said, the experience of making “The Mysterious Production of Eggs” was key to everything he has done since then, even his annual Gezelligheid holiday concerts at Fourth Presbyterian Church. He’s skipping them this year in light of the two Symphony Center dates, but the event will return in 2027. “It had a massive effect on the way I hear music … and that sort of feedback between your environment and what you're playing," he said of one of the takeaways. Another one: “It was a big lesson about the best-laid plans … You have to learn to be more adaptable.” </p><p>Would Bird ever want to give up the polished studio work and the glamorous Hollywood projects to go back to that simple way of creating again? Maybe not. “My life is so different than it was then. … I think what I learned in that period is portable from this point on, and I can take it with me anywhere,” he said. “A sabbatical would be nice though.”</p>

</div><p>In actuality, Jack Johnson was a complicated man. He often skirted the laws of Jim Crow and stayed in whites-only hotels. He only married white women, which eventually led to him to flee the country after being convicted under the Mann Act.</p><p>Even as an athlete, his legacy calls for nuance. His biggest victory, in which he defeated Jeffries, incited race riots that caused the deaths of Black people around the country.</p><p>“The Royale” is an amalgamation of two of Johnson’s fights: a bout with white champion Tommy Burns, and the match with Jeffries, who had retired undefeated and was considered to be the real champion. entries.title: Illinois House speaker's controversies run deep — and were well-known to other powerbrokers in Illinois
entries.summary: <p>As more than one critic of Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch voiced after his announcement that he won’t be running again for the powerful leadership post, his political fall wasn’t as surprising as that it took this long — and that he ever was able to get the job at all.</p><p>Welch’s controversies are extensive, and they date back well before his 2013 arrival in the Legislature representing a west suburban district, a seat the Hillside Democrat apparently plans to retain while stepping away as a House leader.</p><p>He served on the Proviso Township High Schools District 209 board of education from 2001 to 2013, most of that time as president, and faced numerous troubling accusations during that time — most notably that he slammed a former girlfriend’s head against a counter in a Hillside home amid an argument in 2002.</p><p>A police report was filed, but Welch was not charged with a crime and denied committing any violence. His ex-girlfriend has declined to comment.</p><p>The domestic incident was well known at the time Welch was chosen in 2021 to succeed the embattled — and later convicted — Michael Madigan as speaker. While there was some concern raised by legislators such as state Rep. Kelly Cassidy (D-Chicago), the chamber nonetheless voted to make Welch the speaker.</p><p>Cassidy and the National Organization for Women said some sort of review should still be conducted to determine the credibility of the domestic violence complaint. But as the Chicago Sun-Times reported earlier this year, that examination never occurred for reasons that are not clear.</p><p>“I had my concerns in his first election as speaker because the issues had been raised,” Cassidy said. “I gave him the benefit of the doubt the second time around, but it’s not acceptable after what we learned this summer.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-2b0000" name="image-2b0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/77be7f8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5998x3366+0+317/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F86%2F0f%2Fa7d9248c4f0e83694fe48f87937c%2Fwiscabortion-092625-03.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ccfff5f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5998x3366+0+317/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F86%2F0f%2Fa7d9248c4f0e83694fe48f87937c%2Fwiscabortion-092625-03.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e5a9f43/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5998x3366+0+317/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F86%2F0f%2Fa7d9248c4f0e83694fe48f87937c%2Fwiscabortion-092625-03.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="State Rep. Kelly Cassidy speaks at a press conference in Chicago in 2025. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Neither Welch nor his aides responded to requests for comment.</p><h3>Lawsuits allege inappropriate behavior</h3><p>Also during Welch’s time at Proviso, the district faced lawsuits because of alleged inappropriate actions by him, including one filed in 2010 by an employee named Beyonca Johnson who said in court records she was fired after ending a romantic relationship with him and rejecting his advances. </p><p>Johnson was hired by District 209 in 2007, and weeks later “began engaging in a personal and romantic relationship” with Welch, according to her lawsuit.</p><p>She stopped the relationship after several months, yet was “the recipient of his repeated and continual un-welcomed sexual advances,” and “was told by him that her job was gone and that she could kiss her job goodbye.”</p><p>Johnson ultimately was fired, according to her suit. School officials have said she was terminated for not showing up to work as an administrative assistant for the superintendent but she has denied that. The lawsuit was later dismissed by Johnson.</p><p>According to a person familiar with the situation but who asked not to be publicly named, Johnson ended the relationship when she found out Welch was dating another District 209 employee, a high-ranking administrator, at the same time.</p><p>Around the time Johnson filed the lawsuit, and obtained an order of protection, men came to her home and handed the father of Johnson’s child semi-nude photos of Johnson that she’d previously shared with Welch when they were dating, the source said, adding it was interpreted as a threat.</p><p>Johnson unsuccessfully challenged Welch in the Democratic primary in 2012 for the legislative seat being vacated by another Proviso political powerhouse, then-state Rep. Karen Yarbrough (D-Maywood) who went on to become Cook County’s recorder of deeds and clerk before dying in 2024.</p><p>In 2011, another female Proviso employee filed a federal complaint against Welch and the school district alleging retaliation and discrimination stemming from an incident at a football game where the woman said she “failed to hug the president of the board of education when he asked.”</p><p>“That night and the next afternoon, Mr. Emanuel Welch asserted that he was going to make a change in my building because I disrespected him by not hugging him. He sent text messages to my principal to this end.”</p><p>The case was dropped in 2012.</p><p>Also in 2012, a suburban newspaper published a story that said another District 209 employee who had been romantically involved with Welch allegedly lost her job after they broke up.</p><p>The same article said that Welch had “used his influence to help secure employment for at least 13 friends and political supporters and six relatives” at District 209.</p><h3>Allegations of political payback</h3><p>Other lawsuits filed while Welch was at District 209 alleged he engaged in political payback He said he was planning to resign from the board and move, with his young daughter already attending kindergarten in a different community.</p><p>Even though Manzo said Welch and others in District 209 knew this, someone videotaped the girl outside her school, Welch ended up with a copy, and it was played and discussed at a public board meeting. Manzo, who’s now an Oak Brook trustee, said it was a clear attempt by Welch to embarrass and harass him.</p><p>This happened around the time Manzo ran unsuccessfully against Welch’s close political ally, Melrose Park Mayor Ron Serpico.</p><p>“Even the Mafia doesn’t mess with the family,” Manzo said, saying Welch used his daughter “as a weapon.”</p><p>“My 5-year-old daughter had nothing to do with my fight with Welch.”</p><p>Welch later said in a deposition in another lawsuit that he didn’t regret the way he handled that situation, and “that as stewards of the district... it was important entries.title: Your car’s lost its pep? Pop open the hood, maybe a rat’s to blame.
entries.summary: <p>A rat scampers across a grassy patch next to a paved lot at a shopping center in north suburban Niles, picks up a crab apple and carries the bitter little fruit under a parked car and upward — into the engine compartment. </p><p>Soon, the rodent emerges empty-handed and repeats the drill while the vehicle’s owner is inside a nearby storefront, oblivious that a creature is piling up a food source under the hood where there’s also likely a nest — all of which could wreak havoc on expensive auto components over time.</p><p>Not oblivious to this kind of dynamic are local auto mechanics who say rodent infestation in engine compartments is not only common in the Chicago area, but with the weather now turning colder, probably ramping up with rats, mice and other undesirable animals now looking to build a home in a vehicle.</p><p>“It’s the perfect time,” said Joe Santoro, owner of BJ’s Complete Auto Repair at 3820 N. Harlem Ave. “They’re going to be looking.”</p><p>Santoro would know. At the time he was speaking to a reporter over the phone, a Ford pickup truck was at his garage awaiting parts to replace wiring and foam that had been chewed through by what’s likely one or more rats.</p><p>“We’ve been seeing it a lot,” Santoro said. “It’s pretty rampant, it’s been explosive in the last three to five years.”</p><p>“Part of the problem is the rodents in the city,” he said, while another factor is that some auto components are now soy based, which apparently is an attractive food source to voracious rats.</p><p>“I see 2,500 cars a year, I’d say maybe this year I probably saw 40 or 50” vehicles that had some degree of rodent infestation, Santoro said. “It’s not a high percentage, but it’s increasing.”</p><p>Luckily, he’s never encountered live rats in a vehicle, though he’s seen what looks to be active nests — and “we did find some dead ones,” he said.</p><p>Horror stories abound in Chicago of rats making their way into the underbelly of vehicles after a driver parks near dumpsters, a restaurant or some other food source — or even a seemingly safe spot like a residential garage.</p><p>There also have been incidents where rats find their way into the passenger compartment of a car through a window left down and end up burrowing under the floor fabric — a well-known receptacle for crumbs and other bits of food for any motorist with younger kids.</p><p>"The worst one we ever had was a customer of ours, she had two cars, she used one and the other one was left on the street," said Pete Rosquete of Doc Able's Auto Clinic in Evanston. "They got in under the carpeting in the back . . . they made a mess . . . we had to take the back seat out."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-cf0000" name="image-cf0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fadb987/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1702x955+173+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2b%2F02%2Fd0faa96344a3a249bc4b8d6573b9%2F1000036556.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6875384/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1702x955+173+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2b%2F02%2Fd0faa96344a3a249bc4b8d6573b9%2F1000036556.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4ebe187/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1702x955+173+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2b%2F02%2Fd0faa96344a3a249bc4b8d6573b9%2F1000036556.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Chewed wiring inside a vehicle, discovered by mechanics at BJ’s Complete Auto Repair at 3820 N. entries.title: CATCH-22: Cris Collinsworth, Mike Tomlin believe Bears built to go far
entries.summary: <p>Analyzing the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> with the help of 22 names, starting with …</p><p><b>Cris Collinsworth</b> <b>(1)</b>, the NBC color analyst who suffered through the Bears’ sloppy Sunday night — yet walked away a believer.</p><p>“I have a tough time deciding if I’m more impressed with the Bears because <b>Caleb Williams (2)</b> threw the four interceptions and they had five turnovers and they won,” he told me Wednesday. “Or am I worried about Caleb Williams because he had a bad night?”</p><p>He thinks it’s the former. Before Williams threw his first interception — to Bucs safety <b>Tykee Smith (3)</b> at the goal line — he’d started the game 11-for-16 for 145 yards, two touchdowns and a 136.7 passer rating.</p><p>“The first 20 minutes of that game, I don’t know that I’ve ever seen a quarterback play like that,” Collinsworth said. “He could have thrown the ball over his head backward and was going to get a completion of some kind.</p><p>“But I thought it got him right back into some of the bad habits that hurt him his rookie year ... fading away and throwing it up. Because he actually hit a couple of those like that.”</p><p>Despite the disaster Sunday, Williams is one of the most efficient quarterbacks in franchise history. His 95.4 passer rating is the best of any Bears quarterback at their season’s midway point since the league expanded to 17 games in 2021. (And yes, we’ve decided half of 17 games is nine. Call it sportswriter math).</p><p>NFL teams played 16 games per season from 1978-2020. Only five Bears quarterbacks who threw at least 100 balls then had a better passer rating through eight games than Williams does now. Only one had a better passer rating through seven games between 1961-77, when the league played 14 contests.</p><p>Here’s where it gets concerning. No one got better:</p><p>• <b>Jim McMahon</b> <b>(4)</b> had a 107.4 passer rating in the first half of 1984 — and appeared in two games in the second half because of injuries, totaling a 70.6.</p><p>• <b>Erik Kramer (5)</b> had a 101 in 1995 in the first half — and then an 85.8 in the second.</p><p>• <b>Brian Hoyer</b> <b>(6)</b> had a 98 at the midway point of 2016 — and missed the rest of the season with a broken collarbone.</p><p>• <b>Jay Cutler</b> <b>(7)</b> had a 95.8 in the first half of 2014 — and an 80.7 in the second.</p><p>• <b>Rudy Bukich</b> <b>(8)</b> had a 113.7 passer rating in the first half of 1965— and a 81.4 in the second half.</p><p>Only <b>Mitch Trubisky</b> <b>(9)</b> came close to duplicating his first-half success, following a 96.1 in the Bears’ first eight games of 2018 with a 94.4 in the team’s final eight.</p><p>“I think [Williams] just needs to continue what he’s been doing,” <b>Mike Tomlin (10),</b> the Steelers coach-turned NBC analyst, said Wednesday. “Certainly it wasn’t his night the other night against Tampa. But if you just look at the larger picture and trends once he’s come back from injury. They’re up over 30 points per game [the last four games], he’s playing with great confidence. I think he’s still confident in those that he plays with. So I just think it’s upward and onward.”</p><h3>Helping from the other side of the field is …</h3><h3></h3><p>Defensive tackle <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/11/bears-jeffery-simmons-face-voice-defense-tackle-trade-titans-dennis-allen-montez-sweat-sacks-trade-deal-titans" target="_blank" ><b>Jeffery Simmons (11)</b>,</a> for whom the Bears gave up two first-round picks and a third-rounder last month.</p><p>“Even though he’s on the other side of the ball, I think it raises the tide for all parties involved,” Tomlin said.</p><p>Collinsworth’s main question about the Bears before Sunday centered around <b>Jaylon Johnson (12), </b>who has Pro Football Focus’ third-worst coverage grade among cornerbacks who have played half their snaps this season.</p><p>The Bears will give Johnson extra help now that they don’t have to blitz so often. That showed up Sunday, when he intercepted <b>Baker Mayfield (13)</b> and returned the ball 67 yards for a touchdown. The Bears showed blitz but dropped into zone coverage, rushing just four.</p><p>“[Johnson] has struggled a little bit in part because they were having to play so much man coverage,” Collinsworth said. “But now they don’t, because they have Jeffery Simmons. Now they’re gonna have additional help on the back end.”</p><p>The Bears didn’t land the Eagles’ <b>Riq Woolen (14)</b>, the Jets’ <b>Nahshon Wright (15)</b> or any other cornerbacks at the deadline. Collins remains intrigued by the <b>Tyrique Stevenson (16)</b>, <b>Malik Muhammad (17) </b>and <b>Kyler Gordon (18) </b>because they'll benefit from Simmons' pass rush.</p><h3>Credit, then, goes to …</h3><p><b>Ryan Poles (19). </b>Sunday’s dud didn’t discourage Collinsworth and Tomlin from believing the Bears general manager built a Super Bowl-caliber roster.</p><p>“I like the trajectory of that group,” Tomlin said. </p><p>Collinsworth has heard enough about Williams’ preparation that he thinks he’ll put the onus on himself — not coach <b>Ben Johnson (20) — </b>to course correct.</p><p>“I’m a little hard-pressed to name a roster I like a whole lot better than this one …. ” Collinsworth said. “This is a legit team. I do think Caleb will reel it back in a little bit. I really like them.”</p><h3>The biggest bye-week bag of ice goes to …</h3><p>Left guard <b>Joe Thuney (21)</b> and right tackle <b>Darnell Wright (22)</b>, the only two Bears to play every snap on either side of the ball. The Bears have lined up on offense 660 times, the most in the league.</p>

entries.title: Woman killed, white car sought in West Garfield Park hit and run
entries.summary: <p>Police are looking for the driver of a white car that fled the scene after slamming into a 69-year-old woman, killing her Wednesday night in West Garfield Park. </p><p>Around 9:45 p.m., the 69-year-old woman was crossing the street in the 4200 block of West Madison Street when a white sedan struck her, knocking her to the ground, and fled the scene, Chicago police said. </p><p>She suffered severe body trauma and was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital where she died, police said. </p><p>Area 4 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Illinois at No. 4 UCLA a mismatch? In college football this nutty season, there might not be any such thing
entries.summary: <p>In a bonkers <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports" target="_blank" >college football</a> season where up is down, down is up and underdogging it to the tune of a double-digit point spread is just a state of mind, anything can happen.</p><p>If we’ve learned anything on the way to Utah and UCLA being the last two unbeaten teams left in the country, it’s that.</p><p><b>Illinois (+10½) at No. 4 UCLA </b>(8 p.m. Friday, Fox 32, 890-AM) might look on the surface like a mismatch, and maybe it’ll turn out to be one. The Bruins are 9-0 for the first time since 1998, one win from tying the school’s single-season record. They rank second in the Big Ten in offense (to 6-3 Illinois’ ninth) and third in defense (to Illinois’ 15th). A team with seeming magic in its bones — it leads the nation with 17 interceptions and 27 takeaways and is plus-14 in turnovers, and has dusted off an injury to quarterback Nico Iamaleava and won four straight with backup Ty Dieffenbach — just keeps doing whatever it must. First-year leader Bob Chesney is closing in on all the coach of the year awards.</p><p>“This is a very confident football team we’re playing,” Illini coach Bret Bielema said. “Offensively, defensively, special teams, they’re very confident in what they do. They’ve had nothing but great results.”</p><p>Last weekend at Minnesota, the Bruins were tied 17-17 in the fourth quarter before Dieffenbach hit Aidan Mizell for back-to-back 75-yard touchdowns. The senior slinger finished with — go on, have fun doing the math — eight completions for 303 yards.</p><p>“Obviously, that won’t work for us,” Bielema said.</p><p>So, yeah, mismatch?</p><p>Not necessarily. It doesn’t sound possible, but the Illini’s four straight wins ties them for the fourth-longest current streak in the Power 4 conferences. Quarterback Katin Houser is coming off a 292-yard, three-touchdown game against Nebraska in which Collin Dixon — who has a school-record 12 TD catches this season — went off for 129 receiving yards and two more scores. Meanwhile, the defense has come alive, especially in the secondary, since coordinator Bobby Hauck stepped down under enormous pressure in early October and Roger Cooper began pulling the levers.</p><p>This isn’t the same Illini team that lost at home to Purdue. Houser is getting serious attention from the NFL, according to Bielema, and sometimes having the better QB is all it takes to make a game a game. The Illini also played last Friday, giving them an extra day of prep over the Bruins, though a long West Coast trip mitigates that somewhat.</p><p>In Illinois’ first trip to the Rose Bowl in 20 seasons — back when the Granddaddy was still the Granddaddy — an upset would take 2026 from good to great, at least through 10 games. Can it happen? Sure, maybe, possibly. But will it? Bruins, 27-20.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/gqJgSeLIlzE?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Illinois vs. Nebraska | Cinematic Highlights 11/6/26"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>Other Week 11 picks</b></h3><p><i>All games are Saturday. My picks to cover are listed first, with CFP rankings in effect.</i></p><p><b>No. 20 Ohio State (-12½) vs. Northwestern </b>(11 a.m., Fix 32, 720-AM): The Buckeyes are a massively disappointing 6-3, same as the Wildcats (minus the “massively disappointing” part). Both teams are operating without their excellent, but injured, starting QBs. Why can’t the Wildcats win at the Horseshoe for the first time since 1971?</p><p>“We’re not here just to compete,” coach David Braun said. “We’re here to win games.”</p><p>Sounds good. Not happening, though. Buckeyes, 24-7.</p><p><b>No. 18 USC (+10) at No. 9 Indiana </b>(2:30 p.m., CBS 2): Both teams come off a bye week, an advantage to neither side. The Hoosiers are ticked off at having dropped five spots in the rankings without playing, but that doesn’t mean their offensive struggles just go away. Hoosiers by single digits.</p><p><b>No. 23 Arizona (+2½) vs. No. 2 Utah </b>(6:30 p.m., Fox-32): Statistically, these teams are knotted tight. It’s time for Wildcats QB Noah Fifita — a fourth-year starter who has seen it all — to put on a show. Another unbeaten goes down, in keeping with the theme of the season. Wildcats by three.</p><p><b>No. 21 LSU (-4) vs. No. 6 Texas </b>(6:30 p.m., ABC 7): Watch the three-loss Tigers knock off the two-loss Longhorns and let the ridiculous SEC babble about how both teams belong in the playoff begin. LSU, 30-23.</p><p>My favorite favorite: <b>No. 5 Notre Dame (-29½) vs. Boston College </b>(2:30 p.m., NBC 5, 780-AM): This might smell like a trap game to some after the Irish’s hugely important win against Miami, but staying locked in has been a November strength on Marcus Freeman’s watch. entries.title: 'Broadview Six' judge delays potentially explosive hearing featuring top prosecutor's testimony
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="'Broadview 6' judge has to decide whether to hold prosecutors accountable after exposing misconduct " target="_blank" >federal judge</a> who<b> </b>ordered<b> </b>Chicago’s top federal prosecutor and others<b> </b>to testify<b> </b>under oath about the “Broadview Six” case on Thursday<b> </b>pushed back<b> </b>the high-stakes hearing<b> </b>more than two weeks.</p><p>U.S. District Judge<b> </b>April<b> </b>Perry<b> </b>wrote on the court docket that<b> </b>she delayed the hearing until Dec. 2<b> </b>at the request of attorneys in the case, and with the “consent”<b> </b>of the Justice Department. She'd<b> </b>originally<b> </b>scheduled the hearing for Nov. 16.</p><p>The move offers some short-term relief to U.S. Attorney <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/07/chicago-crime-justice-department-doj-boutros-trump-midway-blitz-corruption" target="_blank" >Andrew<b> </b>Boutros</a><b> </b>and three other prosecutors who have been ordered to testify, but uncertainty about the hearing will now hang over their heads throughout the Thanksgiving holiday.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/11/06/broadview-6-hearing-set-to-rock-chicago-federal-courthouse-but-doj-official-could-intervene" >Broadview 6 hearing set to rock Chicago federal courthouse, but DOJ official could intervene</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Two of the prosecutors, Assistant U.S. Attorneys William<b> </b>Hogan<b> </b>and<b> </b>Matthew<b> </b>Skiba, previously asked the judge<b> </b>to delay the hearing<b> </b>so they'd have more time to prepare.</p><p>The news follows a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/11/10/broadview-six-boutros-perry-stanley-woodward" target="_blank" >testy back-and-forth</a> earlier this week between Perry<b> </b>and<b> </b>Associate Attorney General <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/11/06/broadview-6-hearing-set-to-rock-chicago-federal-courthouse-but-doj-official-could-intervene" target="_blank" >Stanley<b> </b>Woodward</a>, who recently took the wheel in the “Broadview Six” litigation. He’s the Justice Department’s third-highest ranking official.</p><p>Woodward<b> </b>on<b> </b>Tuesday<b> </b>questioned<b> </b>Perry’s<b> </b>authority<b> </b>to hold a “mini-trial”<b> </b>over the wreckage of the “Broadview Six” case. On<b> </b>Wednesday, Perry<b> </b>described<b> </b>the feds’<b> </b>“professed lack of clarity”<b> </b>as<b> </b>“immaterial,”<b> </b>pointing to her “inherent authority”<b> </b>to<b> </b>question<b> </b>lawyers<b> </b>who<b> </b>potentially<b> </b>misled her.</p><p>She<b> </b>noted<b> </b>that<b> </b>at least two<b> </b>members of Boutros’ staff — Skiba<b> </b>and<b> </b>Assistant U.S. Attorney<b> </b>Andres<b> </b>Almendarez<b> </b>— have said<b> </b>they<b> </b>are<b> </b>willing<b> </b>to testify, as ordered. </p><p>Still, Woodward<b> </b>argued<b> </b>in a recent<b> </b>court filing<b> </b>that<b> </b>Perry<b> </b>had<b> </b>presented<b> </b>Boutros<b> </b>and his staff “with a Catch-22.”</p><p>“They can testify and risk prosecution,”<b> </b>Woodward said, “or they can assert their rights under the Fifth Amendment and risk antagonizing the court.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/11/10/broadview-six-boutros-perry-stanley-woodward" >Feds question ‘Broadview 6' judge’s authority as clash over top prosecutor’s testimony inches closer</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>It was the second time in six weeks<b> </b>that a Justice Department official<b> </b>left open the possibility that federal prosecutors in Chicago might invoke their Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination.</p><p>Boutros is considered the Chicago area’s top federal law enforcement official. But he and others now face the possibility of sanctions or a criminal contempt finding<b> </b>if Perry believes they lied to her during the failed “Broadview Six” prosecution.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" target="_blank" >The case</a> revolved around a protest outside an immigration holding facility in west suburban Broadview in September 2025. It occurred at the height of the Trump administration’s Operation Midway Blitz deportation campaign.</p><p>But it <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" >collapsed</a> in May after Perry discovered alleged misconduct by Boutros’ staff while seeking an indictment from a grand jury. The initial controversy revolved around the conduct of a veteran rank-and-file prosecutor.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" >What to know about the ‘Broadview Six’ scandal rocking Chicago’s federal courthouse</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>More recently, Perry has turned her attention<b> </b>to potential misstatements made to her by the feds as the case played out.</p><p>The judge<b> </b>told lawyers<b> </b>last month, “my sole focus, at this point, is on lack of candor, concealment of material facts, or other misconduct that occurred before me.”</p>

entries.title: Woman, 48, killed in Greater Grand Crossing hit and run
entries.summary: <p>A woman was killed early Thursday in Greater Grand Crossing, marking the second deadly hit and run in three hours in the city. </p><p>The crash happened around 12:25 a.m. when a 48-year-old woman was hit by a white truck while crossing the street in the 300 block of East 71st Street, Chicago police said. </p><p>The unknown driver of the truck then fled the scene going west, police said. </p><p>She was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center where she was pronounced dead, police said. </p><p>Nearly three hours earlier, a 69-year-old woman was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/12/woman-killed-white-car-sought-in-deadly-west-garfield-park-hit-and-run" target="_blank" >fatally struck</a> by a white sedan that fled the scene in West Garfield Park.</p><p>Detectives are investigating. </p>
