entries.title: Michael Reese developers pitch $10 billion stadium project to lure Bears
entries.summary: <p>A team of Chicago developers unveiled Thursday a $10 billion, 100-acre development plan for the former Michael Reese Hospital site — both as a Hail Mary to keep the Bears in Chicago and hit a city-imposed deadline to submit updated plans. </p><p>The Bears previously <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/bears-stadium/2024/05/16/bears-stadium-lakefront-soldier-field-michael-reese-hospital-site-civic-federation-kevin-warren" >dismissed</a> the Michael Reese site, saying it was too narrow and posed safety concerns because the stadium would have to be built over an active rail line.</p><p>But with Capri Investment Group founder Quintin Primo joining GRIT Chicago, the group of developers and investors led by Farpoint Development that purchased the Michael Reese site, the partners have nearly doubled the size of the proposed Bronzeville Lakefront development. </p><p>They shared grand plans to redevelop a large portion of the South Side into a sports, entertainment and cultural district that would, of course, be anchored by a domed stadium at the widest portion of the trapezoidal-shaped site.</p><p>To further lure the Bears, Capri and its investment partners are willing to purchase the team's Arlington Heights property if the "existing investment there is an obstacle to considering a Chicago location," according to a news release.</p><p>A spokesperson for the development team declined to comment when asked if the updated plans were shared with the Bears ahead of Thursday's announcement.</p><p>A Bears spokesperson declined to comment.</p><p>Renderings by Chicago-based design firm Studio Inference show a glassy 75,000-seat stadium that would host the Bears in addition to other sporting events and concerts. High- and mid-rise buildings surround the stadium, along with a sprawling public park, event stage and youth sports complex, among other features.</p><p>"Our proposal has been designed to address the Bears' needs while creating broader benefits for Chicago," Primo said in a news release. "We believe Bronzeville Lakefront offers the team a compelling stadium and development opportunity, and we are prepared to help resolve the issues that have kept the Bears from seriously considering this location. Most importantly, we believe it can deliver significant long-term value for Illinois taxpayers."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure the project would include the nearby five-building apartment complex <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2019/11/11/20955686/bronzeville-sits-squarely-in-developers-sights" >Prairie Shores</a>, along King Drive between 26th and 31st streets. The property is owned by Golub & Co., who initially purchased it with Farpoint for an estimated $180 million in 2019. </p><p>Golub didn’t respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Plans call for demolishing up to 1,000 units at Prairie Shores during phase one and building about 1,500 apartments. The developers said they would build 1.5 replacement apartments for every existing unit that’s demolished.</p><p>Ald. Lamont Robinson (4th) represents the South Side ward that includes the Michael Reese site, once purchased by the city for an Olympic Village that was never built after the 2016 Summer Games were awarded to Rio de Janeiro.</p><p>“I want to be very clear that before you can remove, tear down Prairie Shores, you have to put the units up first. You need to have 1,000 units up before you can take one unit down or have one family displaced,” Robinson told the Sun-Times. “You have to have someone that is stewarding this. And the commitment is, before you can bring any housing down, you have to have the new property up. That is a commitment that this developer has made.”</p><p>The developers are also proposing a community benefits agreement that would give "priority treatment for affected households to reside in new housing within the district or nearby, rent protections for five years, additional assistance for longer-term residents and oversight by a resident committee and independent monitor."</p><p>"We recognize that redevelopment on this scale raises important questions for the people who already call Prairie Shores home," Zeb McLaurin, founder and CEO of McLaurin Development Partners and a member of GRIT, said in a news release. "Our responsibility is to work with residents to develop a housing program that protects their interests and gives them a meaningful role in shaping what comes next. This project will improve housing opportunities for existing residents, as well as create homes for future generations."</p><p>In total, more than 5,000 homes are expected to be built on-site and in nearby locations, including affordable, senior and student housing. The plan cited Lake Meadows as a potential housing site as well as "early discussions" with Illinois Tech to build on-campus housing.</p><p>It also proposed air rights over the McCormick Place Marshaling Yard to the east and expanding McCormick Place's convention and meeting spaces by 300,000 square feet.</p><p>The Metropolitan Pier and Exposition Authority, which owns McCormick Place, said it supports efforts to boost Chicago's economy.</p><p>"However, the Authority must follow its governing mission as well as adhere to its legislatively mandated procurement procedures. The proposed Bronzeville project may offer interesting opportunities for Chicago, but it is in its early stages. MPEA looks forward to learning more about the plans and discussing it with our clients and community stakeholders. At this time, the Authority has not made any commitments related to the project," an MPEA spokesperson said in a statement.</p><p>What sets the development apart from others attempting to woo the Bears, the developers believe, is that the new stadium will be joined by hotels, recreational facilities and housing that would <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/11/25/chicago-architecture-center-report-urban-stadiums-development" >bring an economic boon</a> to Bronzeville.</p><p>The developers estimate housing, hotels, retail and commercial uses could generate about $135 million in annual tax revenue. They also project approximately $14 billion in regional economic activity during its development, with an estimated 60,000 construction-related jobs.</p><h3>Second chance</h3><p>If the Michael Reese stadium plan has a familiar ring to it, it should.</p><p>In March 2025, developers of the old Michael Reese Hospital site went public with a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/bears-stadium/2025/03/14/bears-stadium-michael-reese-proposal-scott-goodman" >dazzling Hail Mary plan</a> to build a $3.2 billion Bronzeville stadium and an adjacent mixed-use development — with a great lawn extending over Du Sable Lake Shore Drive all the way to Lake Michigan.</p><p>Scott Goodman, principal of Farpoint Development, acknowledged then that he had not met with the Bears, nor had he finalized the financing for the dome or the $600 million in state money needed just to ready the site for development. </p><p>The previous stadium construction cost, estimated at $3.2 billion, was the same amount the Bears assumed in 2024 when team president Kevin Warren <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2024/04/23/bears-new-stadium-dome-lakefront-soldier-field" target="_blank" >stood with Mayor Brandon Johnson to unveil their preferred lakefront stadium proposal</a> on the Museum Campus — a plan that got stuck in the mud in Springfield and could face legal challenges due to the city’s lakefront protection ordinance.</p><p>Robinson acknowledged the Bears have long ago dismissed the Michael Reese site. But he’s all for the idea of including it in the salad bar of Chicago stadium sites for the Bears to consider, along with the site they already own in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/06/bears-stadium-roger-goodell-nfl-commissioner-george-mccaskey-kevin-warren-chicago-arlington-heights-meeting-hammond-indiana" target="_blank" >Arlington Heights</a>.</p><p>“As the alderman of the 4th Ward, I have to develop this site. I cannot leave this site dormant for another 20 years,” Robinson said. “We need more housing and we need to put this back on the rolls for taxes. The city needs resources and we need housing. … As the Bears have stated, they are still looking at sites, and why would we not put everything on the table and have the Bears look at it?”</p><div So many folks can look at it and decide if they’re interested in the site,” Robinson said. “We can’t just do nothing. We have to put plans out there … We gotta develop it. We’ve got to get this thing moving.”</p><p>Bronzeville Lakefront would be a massive public-private undertaking and comes days before lawmakers in Springfield consider financing tools that could sweeten the deal for the Bears to stay in Illinois. </p><p>Capri and GRIT's plan envisions a publicly owned stadium similar to Allegiant Stadium, home of the Raiders. Allegiant is owned by the Las Vegas Stadium Authority and was partially taxpayer-funded through a hotel room tax.</p><p>The developers said the Bears could help foot the bill through the sale of stadium naming rights and personal seat licenses, NFL financing programs and refinancing and issuing Illinois Sports Facilities Authority bonds. It would also count on a mix of municipal, state and federal dollars, as well as tax increment financing, sales tax-backed bonds and transportation funding.</p><p>The development team also said it recently signed a memorandum of understanding with "a major capital provider." </p><p>"The difference between a development vision and a development that gets built is the ability to bring together the land, capital, technical expertise and partnerships needed to execute it," Primo said in a statement. entries.title: Man temporarily trapped on opening day for city's new self-cleaning bathroom in West Town
entries.summary: <p>A man was "temporarily trapped" in the city's new self-cleaning bathroom in West Town Wednesday afternoon. </p><p>A man used the facility at about 3 p.m. and was finished before the door automatically pops open after 15 minutes, Paul Stewart, managing director of Iluminara Public Affairs, said.</p><p>“Everything worked the way it was designed to," said Stewart, saying the unit did not malfunction. </p><p>“Apparently this person didn’t see the button,’’ said Stewart, who added there are actually two buttons that users can push to open the door. There are also audio prompts, which assist users in the unit. </p><p>“They were kicking the door and trying to force the door open,” Stewart said. “They didn’t know how to get out.”</p><p>Those actions also caused the facility, in the 1200 block of North Milwaukee Avenue, to shut down for security purposes, prompting an emergency response from their security personnel and also one of two firehouses in the area who have a key to that unit. </p><p>The fire department responded first, Stewart said, and they were told the person was “agitated,” Stewart said. </p><p>“They flipped the switch and the gentleman came out,” Stewart said.</p><p> The man was not injured, said Stewart, who said the situation was similar to being trapped in an elevator. <br></p>

entries.title: Is truth in documentaries just an illusion? Our new arts podcast debates
entries.summary:
If you have a device that’s connected to the internet, you’ve probably heard about the new documentary “You Can See Everything.” Co-directed by Nathan Fielder (“Nathan for You,” “The Rehearsal”) and Lance Oppenheim (“Primetime,” “Some Kind of Heaven”), the film follows Elizabeth Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, in the 34 days leading up to Holmes prison sentence after she was convicted of defrauding investors at her company, Theranos.

entries.title: Anne Frank exhibit at Griffin Museum of Science and Industry underlines the widespread appeal of denialism
entries.summary: <p>"Holocaust deniers say that her diary was written with a kind of ballpoint pen not available at the time," said Eric Strating, the consul general of the Netherlands in Chicago.</p><p>We were standing in the entrance of<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/04/30/anne-frank-exhibit-at-the-griffin-museum-of-science-and-industry-opens-the-door-to-her-secret-annex" > Anne Frank The Exhibition</a> at the Griffin Museum of Science and Industry, the doomed Dutch teen's handwriting projected on the walls around us.</p><p>I chewed on that information.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-eb0000" name="module-eb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>Give credit to haters. The mental gymnastics they go through. Of course Anne Frank had to be a fraud, because ... why exactly? ... nobody died in the Holocaust? Because it's impossible for a Jewish teen to be sympathetic?</p><p>And the detail of the pen ... genius, with its implication of thorough historical rigor. "We'd like to believe this Frank lie. But our extensive knowledge of the history of pens and ink reveals the hidden hand of the octopoid conspiracy straddling the globe..."</p><p>We need to teach denialism in school. Right now. Not only Holocaust denial — that's just one popular brand of the best-selling denial line of faux intellectual products: climate change denial, medical science denial, humanity of whoever you are given permission to hate denial. People will cling to the most ridiculous suppositions to explain away anything that chafes against their cherished biases.</p><p>If you hate Jews — and who doesn't nowadays? — it can be awkward to have this enormous atrocity, the fruit of that hatred, just sitting there, staring at you out of the pages of history, complete with films, photos and those meticulous German records carefully accounting for every gold filling pried out of the mouths of their victims. So much easier just to say the whole thing never happened.</p><p>"Don't argue with Holocaust deniers," I told the consul general. "It's not intellectual pursuit, but a form of hatred. Nothing you can say is going to make them slap their forehead and go, 'My God, you're right, it <i>did</i> happen!"</p><p>Facts are meaningless to such people. Did you see how Donald Trump reacted to the midterm blowout? A day of rational acceptance. Immediately followed by "it's rigged!" denialism. Followed, when that was hooted down ("Just stop," said Megyn Kelly, of all people) by whatever is coming next. Mutating fantasy in a consequence-free world.</p><p>Actually, lies have consequences. As Anne Frank reminds us. I didn't plan to see the show at the GMSI, which opened in May. I'd already toured the secret annex itself, visiting Amsterdam in 2023, and taken away its grim lessons — totalitarianism rises, innocent, ordinary people are caught between the gears and crushed, thanks the genius of their friends and neighbors at denying their humanity based on lies. </p><p>Plus, I have complicated feelings about Frank, which I expressed last month in a column about Polish poet <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/10/20/polish-poet-turns-words-of-holocaust-victims-perpetrators-into-shards-of-memory-activism" target="_blank" >Grzegorz Kwiatkowski</a>:</p><p>"Over the years, we’ve seen the Holocaust transformed into entertainment, especially on social media. Once there was one Anne Frank. Now there are 6 million. The Holocaust has been retrofitted into a bracing tale of courage, resistance, and redemption. The Holocaust is not a tale of courage, resistance and redemption. It is an epic of cruelty, obedience and horror."</p><p>This was seen at the Netherlands Consulate General in Chicago as perhaps throwing shade upon their national heroine, and they invited me to accompany Consul General Strating through the exhibit. He was generally silent, as diplomats tend to be — but not as mum as another Chicago consul general I had lunch with last week. Though he represents a small Middle Eastern nation currently being grilled on both sides by the flames of international opprobrium, he said nothing on the record and nothing off the record of any value except for creating the general impression that his superiors really don't understand the predicament they've dug themselves into. Denialism comes in many flavors.</p><p>The Anne Frank show runs through Jan. 31, and is comprehensive and excellent, a must-see, particularly for those who won't find their way to Amsterdam eventually.</p><p>After touring the show, we went in search of the Dutch national Christmas tree, one of more than 50 trees in the GMSI's "Christmas Around the World" extravaganza. We found it.</p><p>The placard told about the feast of Sinterklaas, Dec. 5 in the Netherlands, and how "On this day, children put out shoes filled with hay and carrots for Sinterklaas' horses hoping to find them filled with treats in the morning."</p><p>"Santa Claus only has one horse," said Strating, relating how, as a child, he had a gray horse, and was pressed into the Sinterklaas role. I smiled, thinking of the ball point pen canard that began our conversation. People are so punctilious, under most circumstances. Unless the facts cut against their biases. Then they untether the slavering beasts of their imagination and let them roam free. The results speak for themselves.</p>

entries.title: Man charged with shooting that left 4-year-old girl wounded
entries.summary: <p>A Chicago man is scheduled to appear in court Thursday, charged in a shooting that left a 4-year-old wounded in Auburn Gresham. </p><p>Patrick Wallace, 30, was charged with possessing a weapon as a felon, causing a child to be endangered and violating an order of protection, Chicago police said. </p><p>He was scheduled to appear in court Thursday. </p><p>The girl was in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/11/girl-4-shot-in-auburn-gresham" target="_blank" >8200 block of South Hermitage Avenue</a> about 9:05 a.m. Wednesday when she was shot in her hand, according to police.</p><p>She was taken to Comer Children’s Hospital in good condition. No one else was hurt, police said.</p>

entries.summary: <p>Ferrara Candy Co. cerrará su planta de producción en La Villita y despedirá a más de 150 empleados en abril.</p><p>La compañía anunció planes para cerrar su instalación en la calle 31st en abril de 2027, citando "las condiciones del mercado y nuestra hoja de ruta de innovación a largo plazo".</p><p>Funcionarios notificaron a 154 empleados y al estado la semana pasada y dijeron que planean trasladar la producción a otras plantas. La planta está ubicada en 2945 W. 31st St.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-960000" name="module-960000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>"Ferrara está profundamente agradecida con la comunidad de La Villita de Chicago por años de asociación y colaboración comunitaria", dijo la compañía en un comunicado.</p><p>Ferrara, cuyas marcas incluyen SweeTARTS, Brach’s y Nerds, comenzó como una panadería en el vecindario de Little Italy en 1908 y ha operado en Chicago durante casi 120 años.</p><p>El fabricante de confitería fue adquirido por Ferrero en 2017, pero permanece como una empresa privada bajo propiedad común. Ferrara opera otras tres instalaciones de fabricación en el área de Chicago —en Bellwood, Forest Park e Itasca— y una cuarta en DeKalb.</p><p>Ferrara dijo que los empleados podrán seguir trabajando en la planta hasta su cierre. Los trabajadores también tienen la oportunidad de postularse a puestos vacantes en Ferrara y en su red de afiliadas.</p><p>La compañía dijo que ofrecerá prestaciones por despido y servicios de recolocación para ayudar a los empleados afectados a encontrar nuevos trabajos.</p><p>La semana pasada se informó a los empleados sobre el cierre planeado, en cumplimiento de la Ley Worker Adjustment and Retraining Act (WARN), dijo Ferrara.</p><p>La Ley WARN de Illinois exige que las empresas con 75 empleados o más notifiquen a los trabajadores y al estado con al menos 60 días de antelación antes de cierres de planta o despidos masivos.</p><p>No es la primera vez que Ferrara cierra una planta de fabricación.</p><p>En 2024, la compañía cerró su planta de Jelly Belly en North Chicago, despidiendo a 66 empleados menos de un año después de haber adquirido la empresa familiar Jelly Belly por una cantidad no divulgada.</p><p>Ese mismo año, Blommer Chocolate Co. anunció que cerraría su fábrica en West Town, recortando 250 empleos debido al aumento de los costos de operar la antigua instalación en 600 W. Kinzie St.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Bulls suffer blow as Caleb Wilson to miss 4-6 weeks with hand injury
entries.summary: <p>It’s starting to feel like the Bulls just can’t have nice things.</p><p>A right-hand injury forced prized rookie Caleb Wilson out of the game against the Spurs in the third quarter, and testing on Thursday revealed more bad news as he required surgery that will sideline him for the next four to six weeks.</p><p>Not only a huge blow for the franchise and the No. 4 overall pick, but also a tough hill for him to climb in the Rookie of the Year campaign he was hoping to make a run at.</p><p>Not exactly what a 1-9 team needed right about now.</p><p>The 20-year-old was averaging 18.9 points, 6.2 rebounds and 1.9 assists per game, shooting 32.4% from three-point range. He was also putting together a strong showing against San Antonio, scoring 15 minutes in 15 minutes of work before he tried swiping the ball out of Victor Wembanyama’s hand and suffered the injury.</p><p>Not the only thing that went wrong for the Bulls in that third quarter, but definitely the most significant. The gut-punch in the Wilson news was he was questionable before the game with a sore right hip and wanted to gut through it.</p><p>Exactly what the Bulls were doing, playing one of their better first halves of the season and leading the defending Western Conference Champions by as much as 22. That is until the third-quarter meltdown — a reoccurring theme for the team.</p><p>“We’re in a league where you either win or you lose,” veteran Jalen Smith said of the on-going issues. “We’re 1-9 now? So as a young team it’s demoralizing because you want to win every game, but you’ve got to understand that there is a process to it and we’ve got to put together a whole 48 (minutes). We can’t pick and choose when we want to play hard. We are in a rebuild, we have a bunch of young guys trying to learn a new system, new coach, new front office, and everyone is doing their part, but we just got to put together a win.”</p><p>Just the latest reminder of how painful rebuilds are.</p><p>The other reality staring this team in the face? Yeah, they want to “put together a win,” but are they prepared to play the right way for four quarters and who does it come against?</p><p>It’s not like the schedule is allowing them to take a breath, facing Atlanta, Minnesota and Cleveland the next three. There’s a realistic chance they go into Brooklyn on Nov. 18 with a 1-12 record, hoping to end the streak against the 3-8 Nets. Maybe. With Wilson down that becomes tougher.</p><p>It starts with ball security and understanding the importance of coming out of the halftime locker room with the same intensity they have started some of these games.</p><p>“The first five minutes of the third quarter is the most important part of any game, whether you’re down 20 or up 20,” forward Matas Buzelis said.</p><p>That’s why he was so hard on himself after the Spurs loss.</p><p>He had a stellar first half and watched it quickly turn into a nightmare, thanks to a scoreless third in which he turned the ball over four times.</p><p>“To be honest it’s on me,” Buzelis said. “I’m one of the leaders on this team and I have to be able to fight in the third quarter. I came out like dragging and good teams like that, they take advantage. I have to be way better and I will be.”</p><p>Buzelis will need to be as the focus now turns back to him with Wilson out. Year 3 for the forward was supposed to give more clarity on his place as a foundation piece, but he’s been inconsistent through the first 10 games.</p><p>There is now a clearer runway for Buzelis to find more shots but that doesn’t come close to softening the blow of losing Wilson.</p>

entries.title: After breakthrough 2026, White Sox look to avoid a letdown in 2027
entries.summary: <p>LAS VEGAS — Will Venable received <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/11/10/white-sox-will-venable-named-al-manager-of-the-year" target="_blank" ><u>an award for the 2026 season this week</u></a>, but he started thinking about 2027 weeks ago. The post mortem of how the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> fell short in the American League Division Series immediately bled into how it could be made better next year.</p><p>“There’s likely a lockout, we’re not going to be able to communicate with our players, so very quickly the focus begins on how to get better,” Venable said. “These guys were very disappointed that things ended the way that they did. They're very driven, very motivated already, but now they have more fuel to go out and have a really, really good offseason.”</p><p>A funny thing happened between the Houston Astros cracking the playoffs in 2015 with a young core of Jose Altuve, Carlos Correa and George Springer, and their streak of seven-straight ALCS appearances that began in 2017 — their patchwork pitching staff scuffled and they missed the playoffs with an 84-78 record in 2016.</p><p>If a successful rebuilding journey to perennial contention can take backwards steps, why would the White Sox be immune, least of all as they too try to upgrade their patchwork pitching staff? Maybe there won’t be 11 walk-off victories next season, maybe the right-handed platoon bat they pick up won’t lead MLB in slugging against lefties again, maybe the AL won’t be weak again in 2027.</p><p>“Is it possible? Sure,” said general manager Chris Getz. “Injuries happen. It’s the major leagues. It's very competitive. You got other teams that are making improvements and adding to their club.”</p><p>The White Sox intend to do their part in that regard with their starting pitching pursuit. The rotation is the roster’s weak point and the strongest area of the free-agent crop, and the most efficient way to use their available, but still-limited provided budget compared to other major-market teams.</p><p>“It's the greatest need in our game, but there's opportunities out there, there's opportunities in this free agent class, there's going to be opportunities in trades,” Getz said. “There definitely could be opportunities that we go for a lengthier contract for a pitcher. It hasn't made sense for us to do that. Is now the time? Perhaps.”</p><p>This approach puts less pressure on the likes of Noah Schultz and David Sandlin to make big leaps forward to give the Sox a playoff-caliber rotation. But it comes alongside the hope that internal development can do the heavy lifting of the lesser task of filling out the bullpen around Hagen Smith, who has the best chance of ascending to a 2026 Grant Taylor-like relief role.</p><p>Getz alluded to the bullpen being how they retain out-of-options pitchers, which could enable major-league roles for Jonathan Cannon and Chris Murphy. Bryan Hudson and Anthony Kay also are out of options. Inevitably some arms will arrive in spring–whenever that is–stretching out for a starting role, but will settle into multi-inning relief, which feels like a reasonable projection for hard-throwing righties Tanner McDougal and Shane Smith after rocky 2026 campaigns. The Sox lack pitching depth between the majors and their most recent draft crop, but Pierce George and Matthias LaCombe are relief prospects who could help by midseason, and lefty trade acquisition Jaden Woods was briefly considered as a call-up late last year, and could be protected on the 40-man roster next week.</p><p>Contact wizard infielder William Bergolla Jr. is the other expected 40-man addition by Tuesday’s deadline, having completed his running progression after a right fibular stress fracture that ended his 2026 season. After 40 homers across the minors and the Arizona Fall League, Caleb Bonemer and Bergolla represent the team’s clearest sources of internal upgrades on the position side.</p><p>But avoiding a step back, balancing out their offense’s contact issues and deepening their pitching options still largely rests upon how the arms sidelined from the postseason pitching plan respond, how Braden Montgomery works to tap into his still unrealized potential, how <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/25/white-sox-shortstop-colson-montgomery-offensive-struggles-jake-burger-will-venable-derek-shomon-jacob-degrom-all-star-home-runs" target="_blank" ><u>Colson Montgomery responds to a second half slide</u></a>.</p><p>“He’s hungry right now,” Getz said of his shortstop. “We look forward to seeing how this plays out.”</p>

entries.title: The Sky need a point guard of the future. They should explore trading for Juste Jocyte
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/11/12/illinois-ucla-illini-bruins-rose-bowl-pasadena-big-ten-college-football-picks" target="_blank" >Sky</a> need a point guard of the future. That’s one thing the front office and its fans can agree on.</p><p>Look around the league and it’s the young crop of PG’s running the show — Caitlin Clark, Olivia Miles, Paige Bueckers, and Veronica Burton.</p><p>Courtney Vandersloot, the Sky’s starting point guard, still has sublime moments representative of her Hall of Fame career, and for a 37-year old recovering from an ACL injury, her 2026 campaign was impressive. But she’s no longer a top eight point guard in the league.</p><p>The Sky’s other two point guards are in the 35+ crowd and may or may not be back in 2027 — Natasha Cloud is a free agent and Skylar Diggins could be traded.</p><p>Finding a point-guard-of-the-future is clearly a priority for general manager Jeff Pagliocca.</p><p>“We’re going to keep building that young core,” Pagliocca said in his exit interview. “We have posts. We have wings. We will add a point guard to it at some point. I think that’s fair to say that we’ll be looking at a young point guard.”</p><p>He’ll have to be creative about getting a great one<b>.</b> Franchise-changing talent at the position is usually found in the draft lottery, but the Sky consistently deal away their own picks in “win-now” moves. They gave up the pick that became Miles to the Lynx earlier this year. </p><p>They’ll feel the pain again on Sunday night, when the 2027 lottery order will be determined. Because of a previous trade with Washington, the Sky’s pick, wherever it lands, will belong to the Mystics.</p><p>That means no chance at drafting the best point guard in the college game, Notre Dame senior Hannah Hidalgo. The Mystics also own the Sky's 2028 first-round pick. </p><p>So the Sky will have to focus on less traditional paths, like finding a hidden gem overseas or in the later stages of the draft. Think a point guard version of All-Rookie team guard Sydney Taylor.</p><p>They’ll also need to pounce when trade opportunities arise. Surprisingly, one could be developing with the champs.</p><p>The Valkyries former lottery pick, 20-year-old Juste Jocyte, told Lithuanian outlets this week that she’s looking for a trade out of Golden State. Jocyte didn’t crack the Valkyries rotation in her rookie season and took issue with coach Natalie Nakase’s communication about her role.</p><p>This news should send Pagliocca to the batphone ASAP.</p><p>Though not a natural point guard, Jocyte has excellent vision and a sweet lefty stroke. The Valkyries didn’t really capitalize on that — in their isolation-heavy offense, Jocyte often ended standing up in the corner. She might be a better fit for Sky coach Tyler Marsh’s offense, which features more ball movement and creativity.</p><p>In a best case scenario, Jocyte would learn under Vandersloot, transitioning from shooting guard to become the Sky’s point-guard-of-the-future. Even in a medium-case scenario where she sticks to the wing, adding a young shooter with high upside can’t hurt.</p><p>The opportunity here is that Jocyte's trade value shouldn't be too rich given her limited role, and the Sky have some non-lottery draft capital to offer. They received the Dream’s 2027 and 2028 first-round picks when they traded All-WNBA forward Angel Reese. One of those picks might be enough to get Jocyte.</p><p>Being on the receiving end of a player wanting out would be a nice break for the Sky!</p><p>For too long trade requests have hurt their momentum. Since inheriting the GM role in 2023, Pagliocca has had to honor requests from presumed franchise pillars Kahleah Copper and Marina Mabrey. The Reese trade was in a slightly different category because each side called it “mutual” rather than an official request, but she’d clearly lost faith in the franchise.</p><p>If the Sky could nab Jocyte for cheap, it would help offset some of the damage from the Reese deal, and help establish a new trend of players landing in, rather than leaving, Chicago.</p><p>The Jocyte situation isn’t perfect. A r<a class="Link" href="https://clutchpoints.com/wnba/golden-state-valkyries/valkyries-news-juste-jocytes-future-golden-state-uncertain-candid-comments-lithuanian-media" target="_blank" >eport from ClutchPoints</a> this week suggested she wasn’t thrilled about the Valkyries plan to turn her into a point guard, and in her recent interviews, she didn’t sound 100% sure she even wants to play in the United States. Her priority in the summer has been the Lithuanian national team.</p><p>The Sky will need to do their diligence first. But given that they'll be kissing their lottery pick goodbye Sunday night, these are the kinds of situations they must explore.</p>

entries.title: Blackhawks could use more of the elements Andrew Mangiapane brings
entries.summary: <p>Two of Andrew Mangiapane's best traits happen to fall in two categories where the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> need the most improvement.</p><p>They <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/09/blackhawks-systems-changes-jeff-blashill-wyatt-kaiser-defense" >spent all week</a> working on their forecheck pressure and backcheck tracking, acknowledging they haven't recovered enough dump-ins or forced enough turnovers in the offensive zone and they've especially given up too many odd-man rushes due to ineffective forechecks.</p><p>And they've talked for several weeks now about being more physical and tough to play against, including battling tenaciously for pucks and wearing down opponents in addition to dishing out hits.</p><p>Mangiapane, meanwhile, is one of the Hawks' few veteran forwards who's both fast enough and scrappy enough to move the needle on both fronts.</p><p>Yes, the 30-year-old winger isn't the offensive producer he used to be, but his nose for the puck and the net hasn't faded.</p><p>He still skates well, plays a direct north-south game and knows how to use his undersized 5-10 body to his advantage along the boards. He's willing to throw it around sometimes, too, and he's happy to ignite or jump into post-whistle scrums.</p><p>He even showed some of that feisty nature in practice Monday, barking at Hawks defenseman Sam Rinzel for a dangerous — albeit accidental — check behind the net. There were no hard feelings afterward.</p><p>So it's perplexing why Mangiapane hasn't been involved more in the Hawks' game plans so far this season. </p><p>Since getting cleared to return from injury Oct. 23, he has bounced in and out of the lineup. Entering Thursday, he had dressed four times — averaging about 11 minutes of ice time in those four games — and had been a healthy scratch five times.</p><p>He played well in his limited minutes, with the Hawks outshooting opponents 19-15 and outscoring them 2-1 during his five-on-five ice time. His line with Anton Frondell and Tyler Bertuzzi was dominant on Oct. 31 against the Bruins and decent again Nov. 2 against the Avalanche. Yet they were split apart throughout the Hawks' disastrous road trip. </p><p>Mangiapane finally returned to Frondell's line Thursday, this time opposite Patrick Kane. Ideally, this will mark the start of a genuine opportunity for him to find a niche on this struggling roster.</p><p>"He's definitely a guy who plays with energy and a guy who can create turnovers," coach Jeff Blashill said. "He's had a fairly small sample size with us, period. I’m still learning him as a player, totally.</p><p>"So, can he bring that? I think he can. He’s had some good moments in games, for sure. Hopefully he can continue to build more and more moments."</p><p>Mangiapane said this week he feels good physically, which hasn't been the case much lately (considering he played hurt all of last season).</p><p>He also said these three consecutive practices sharpened his understanding of the Hawks' systems, which is exactly what Blashill hoped would happen.</p><p>It's crucial to operate as a five-man unit on the forecheck, for example, with each guy fulfilling his role within the 2-1-2 structure. The Hawks have been failing on that front frequently.</p><p>"Everyone's mind has to be there," Mangiapane explained. "[You] can't be too early, because then they're not going to pass it to that guy. And [you] can't be too late, because the guy's going to have too much time. I don't think it's about speed. It's about meeting the puck at the same time.</p><p>"Maybe you're just trying to force the puck to another area so that your teammate can kill the play. And that's where you've got to be on the same page. Forechecking takes all five guys...because in this league, they'll just keep bumping it to the open guy. And if one guy is not there, that's when the breakdown happens."</p><p>We'll see moving forward if Mangiapane can help the Hawks execute it as well as he can explain it.</p>

entries.title: Jason Dónes wins tight race for District 3b Chicago School Board seat
entries.summary:
District 3b neighborhoods: Humboldt Park, Logan Square, Belmont Cragin, West Town, Hermosa

Jason Dónes has upset incumbent Carlos Rivas Jr. by about 4 percentage points, adding another win for a Chicago Teachers Union-backed candidate in the historic school board election, according to Chicago Board of Election data.

As elections officials continued to count mail-in and provisional ballots, Dónes declared victory in the Near Northwest Side race in social media posts Tuesday.

"This victory belongs to the parents, educators, students, working families and neighbors who believe that our schools should answer to our communities — not the wealthy interests willing to spend whatever it takes to influence them," he said on Instagram.

It took until Nov. 5 for elections officials to count all the precincts in the school board district, and the results showed Dónes with a small lead over Rivas, a former-teacher-turned city communications director, that continued to grow as each new batch of votes came in. It was about 1,100 votes as of Thursday. By Nov. 12, when Chicago Public Media called the race, Dónes' lead roughly matched that of other leading candidates at the time the news organization called their races.

Election officials have until Nov. 17 to finish counting mail-in ballots and provisional ballots. Final official results are to be released on Nov. 24.

It's was a rematch for two men who both grew up in Humboldt Park, graduated from selective-enrollment Chicago public high schools, and became teachers through Teach for America. In 2024 Rivas Jr. won with 54% of the vote.

Both candidates identify as progressives. Rivas, who did not return messages for comment, has taken a more fiscally conservative approach to the school budget than his opponent.

Bolstered by about $600,000 from groups that oppose the Chicago Teachers Union, Rivas also had support from the Service Employees International Union, which represents thousands of CPS school support staff and has split politically with the teachers union in recent years. Also behind him were charter school advocates, some Northwest Side officials and the the Common Ground Collective, a political action committee that opposes the CTU, is heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks and says it aims to engage voters around “effective progressive policies.”

Dónes was backed by the CTU and several Northwest Side elected officials.

A few days before the election, Rivas responded to the release of records that showed he was suspended from his job at a charter school in 2018 after he became intoxicated at a work event and engaged in “unwanted touching” of a co-worker.

Rivas said the incident happened at a difficult time in his life when he was caring for his dying mother and that he took responsibility for what happened and got help through an employee assistance program.

“I believe in accountability, growth and second chances,” he told the Chicago Sun-Times in a statement. Rivas worked as a teacher, college counselor and external affairs manager at the school. He is now the public affairs director for the Civilian Office of Police Accountability.

Schools in District 3b are struggling with teacher and counselor shortages, higher property taxes, and low enrollment amid rapid gentrification. The district includes a mix of 32 schools serving mostly Latino students. The schools are generally strong, with about 60% achieving the state’s second highest rating last year. But 6% have the lowest of the five ratings.

Rivas and Dónes both care about protecting immigrant students from federal immigration agents, supporting more affordable housing, and securing more resources and community partnerships for CPS families. Rivas says he wants less interference from the mayor on the board and to move away from using loans that will increase CPS’ budget deficit.

Dónes, a CPS parent, was looking to increase budget transparency, push for creative solutions within the existing budget framework, and said on our questionnaire that he wouldn’t accept contributions from corporations or “private interest groups funded by billionaires and millionaires.”

Rivas’ outside support was about five times greater than Dónes’. As of Monday, more than half of the $502,000 backing Rivas came from the political arm of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools while another $123,000 came from the anti-CTU Common Ground Collective. All of Dónes’ outside support comes from the CTU, totaling about $22,000.

Contributing: Ariel Parrella-Aureli of Block Club Chicago and Kate Grossman

entries.title: Chicago Thanksgiving Parade to start an hour earlier for the first time in 92 years
entries.summary: <p>If you're planning to attend the Chicago Thanksgiving Parade this year, set your alarm an hour earlier.</p><p>For the first time in the parade's 92-year history, the procession will begin at 7:45 a.m. on Thanksgiving morning — an hour earlier than in previous years, according to a parade spokesperson who confirmed the change to the Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>The earlier start will allow the parade's television broadcast to begin at 8 a.m. on CBS Chicago, ahead of the Chicago Bears' Thanksgiving Day matchup against the Detroit Lions. Pregame coverage will follow at 10 a.m.</p><p>The parade will take place Thursday, Nov. 26, along State Street, starting at Ida B. Wells Drive and proceeding north to Randolph Street. Admission is free.</p><p>Other changes to this year's celebration include a Chicago Bears legend as grand marshal, according to a news release.</p><p>Charles “Peanut” Tillman, the former Bears cornerback who played 12 seasons with the team, will serve as grand marshal.
